articles.headline: Everything you need to know about WoW Forever leveling
keyFacts: World of Warcraft: Forever features a Level 60 level cap and keeps the original experience curve, according to developers.
Players earn experience through quests, monster kills, and discoveries, while group play and rested states offer additional leveling bonuses.
Developers added new regions like Riverglades and Shen'Dralas to help alleviate the difficult leveling grind around Level 40.
body: World of Warcraft: Forever welcomes everyone to Azeroth for the first time for, well, the third time. And anyone who’s built a career out of creating alts throughout Retail and in Classic would want to just go through the motions and get to Level 60 ASAP to enjoy all the new endgame features WoW: Forever has to offer.

But with Level 60 as the capstone, it’s not going to be as quick a ride compared to other WoW expansions. And if this is your first time dipping your toes into an intense MMO like WoW , here’s a quick lesson in leveling in Forever.
Table of contents
Is the journey to Level 60 going to be a boring ride?
Always an upward progression
But first, learn about tagging
Tackle leveling by quest area
Rested XP literally rewards you for taking a breather
Dungeon quests give more XP, dungeon mobs give less
Level 40 is still the biggest (most frustrating) part of the grind
Strictly Level 60 is a first for Blizzard
Is the journey to Level 60 going to be a boring ride?

For an MMO that lets characters experience the highs of being Level 120 (back in Battle for Azeroth , at least), Level 60 for Forever feels awfully fast. Or the worse alternative, the mid-point grind will probably be horrifyingly slow.

“We did not change the experience curve,” Kris Zierhut, WoW: Forever ‘s principal designer told Sean Keach of The Sun . “So what we’ve really done is just created a different path. The experience curve remains the same.”
Blizzard devs also highlighted this with similar metrics from the WoW: Forever Beta. The average leveling time from Level 1 to 20 in Classic is 20.4 hours, compared to 20.5 in the Forever Beta.

“The big intent is to get you into the world and keep you in it,” Josh Greenfield, WoW: Forever senior game designer, said in the WoW: Forever podcast. “Part of the game is to protect and nurture social experiences. We want to keep you in the world as much as possible.”
But what does this mean for the rest of the leveling experience?
Always an upward progression

Leveling in WoW: Forever is standard-fare RPG mechanics. You get XP by turning in quests, killing mobs, and discovering new areas. For monsters specifically, you get more XP by fighting higher-level mobs compared to lower-level ones.
From your starting zone, expect that quests will eventually get you to a nearby zone with mobs scaled to your general level.

Expect to encounter more lower-level mobs in starting zones to help get you up to speed. Then they get less and less the more you level up. Blizzard said they’ll squeeze in extra spawn rates during launch and will balance things out eventually.
But first, learn about tagging
Leveling can get confusing when other people get involved. If you’re in a high-population area, chances are there are a lot more people also farming the same mobs. This is where tagging comes in.
Basically, if you tag or attack the monster first, you get first dibs on the XP. The monster’s name turns gray for them, which means someone else is already actively engaging the monster.
Even if they kill the monster, you get the XP. The same works if you kill a mob someone already tagged; this time they get the XP instead of you.
If this seems too confusing, you can always just buddy up.
When grouping, go for quests

No adventurer is an island, and one of the M’s in MMORPG does stand for “multiplayer,” so WoW: Forever does incentivize group play. When you party up with other players, you share any XP you get from killing mobs.

At first glance, this seems counterintuitive since you can just earn more if you kill them solo. But the idea is that you can theoretically tackle more powerful mobs and earn even more XP just because you’re in a team.
Plus, you don’t share Quest XP, so it helps to tackle zones together as a unit.
Alternatively, instead of buddying up, just take turns getting first tag on a monster. Everyone else helps, but the tagger gets the XP. Then rotate.
But take note that the higher-level the “helper,” the less XP the tagger will get.
What about leveling up Professions?

Professions are leveled separately. Basically, things you do that actively involve the Profession will earn XP for it. After reaching a certain level, you have to rank up your Profession via the Trainer in order to access more benefits and potential craftable items.
Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter !
Tackle leveling by quest area

World of Warcraft: Forever map showing nearby quest areas via the Questie add-on. Image and remix by Destructoid One of the fastest ways to tackle quests in WoW: Forever is the ages-old strategy of doing it zone by zone. Blizzard built Azeroth in such a way that quests will have you naturally go from one area to the next until such a point that you can choose whichever common-leveled zones you want to spend time in.

With an add-on like Questie , you can have a rough estimate of the claimable quests in the zone you’re in and gauge your plan from there. The usual strategy is to accept all quests in one zone, do everything in the vicinity, then turn in everything at once. By the time a quest sends you to the next zone, that’s the sign it’s time to move on.
Rested XP literally rewards you for taking a breather

When you stay in a safe location like an inn, a city, or even with the Cozy Sleeping Bag, you’ll end up in something called a rested state. In here, you start to accumulate something called Rested XP .

This is a concept taken straight from Classic . You know you’re there when your XP bar becomes blue instead of purple. As long as you’re eligible for Rested XP, you gain double the XP from monster kills. This eligibility depends on a “stockpile” of XP you accumulate as you stay rested. Here are other things to consider:
You stockpile 5% of your level for every 8 hours you spend rested, up to 150% of your current level
When you kill a monster while rested, the XP earned will be reduced from whatever stockpile you earned
If you’re not killing mobs, you’re not using Rested XP (quest turn-ins, Profession progress, exploration XP)
Always set your Hearthstone in an inn. If you have to log out at any point, you’ll have accumulated some Rested XP by the time you come back.
Dungeon quests give more XP, dungeon mobs give less

Since Forever is in part a reimagining of the vanilla WoW launch, it’s no surprise vets will have a specific leveling approach in mind. It’s a ritual at that point, especially for those who have an alt for just about any situation.
But take note that part of Blizzard’s plan is to focus less on farming mobs and doing more quests.
“Moving a lot of that experience (leveling) off of just the kills and onto the quests really incentivizes you to do that (the quests) at least once,” Greenfield said on the WoW: Forever podcast.
This also goes for dungeons, where dungeon quests now give more XP while dungeon mobs give less. Prioritize clearing dungeon quests for the first time, as this is where the most XP gain happens.
Level 40 is still the biggest (most frustrating) part of the grind

Anyone who’s ever tried leveling a character in Classic will be intimately familiar with the dreaded Level 40 grind. It’s just a point in anyone’s adventuring career where quests are scarce, and there’s really no “logical” point of zoning progression.

Back in the day, your choices beyond the questlines would be bouncing to and from your preferred farming zones. Forever wants to solve this by adding a couple more regions (and theoretically, quests) to help with that grind:
Riverglades: Imagine Stranglethorn Vale, hopefully with enough quests and fodder to satisfy the mid-30s to mid-40s grind
Shen’Dralas: Mid-to-high-level bracket situated between Desolace, Feralas, and Mulgore
These zones will be new additions to staple zones of this level, such as:
Early 40s : Feralas, Tanaris
Mid 40s: Searing Gorge, The Hinterlands
Late 40s: Badlands, Blasted Lands, Un’Goro Crater
Strictly Level 60 is a first for Blizzard
Logging into World of Warcraft: Forever to see a Level 60 cap might make it feel… lacking for some reason. Level 60 always felt like the midpoint to something else, not really a capstone digit.
It could have been the history. WoW: Forever is pegged as a reimagining of the 2004 Vanilla launch, which did have the Level 60 cap.

But then again, it only took two years before The Burning Crusade raised that to Level 70. Come 11 years later, Battle for Azeroth gave us a monumental peak of Level 120, then Shadowlands squished everything back to Level 60. Then Blizzard just couldn’t get its hands off the max level, so here we are at Midnight , a couple more expansions later, with a Level 90 cap.

Basically, it felt un -Blizzard for them to declare WoW: Forever to be strictly until Level 60. If they keep the promise, leveling will be more interesting if they follow through by introducing more routes for that midpoint grind. And if they somehow start pushing the meter again, none of us would be really surprised.
World of Warcraft: Forever is out right now for PC and macOS.
The post Everything you need to know about WoW Forever leveling appeared first on Destructoid .

articles.headline: Xbox enters the 'faster PC launcher' arms race, its app loads faster now too
keyFacts: Xbox announced an updated Xbox PC app for Insiders that launches up to 60 percent faster.
Xbox said home, store, and Game Pass pages load up to 50 percent faster with simplified navigation.
Users can access the updated app by installing the Xbox Insider Hub.
body: Xbox has joined the 'faster launcher load times' arms race, announcing that its updated Xbox PC app, available now to Xbox Insiders, launches up to 60% faster, and has also been overhauled to offer "simpler navigation, updated filters, and new ways to organize your games."

Along with the faster launch time, Xbox said the home, store, and Game Pass pages in the updated app load up to 50% faster, while in-app windows open up to 65% faster—depending upon factors including device, internet connection, system configuration, and usage, of course. Library navigation has been simplified, search has been improved, and friends and social features are now part of the main navigational window.

Credit where it's due: That change to friends and social features is welcome. I don't use the Xbox App much—to be blunt, it's pretty much exclusively for Sea of Thieves. But after a long stretch away from it, I recently jumped back in for some high seas adventures with the crew, and I'll tell you this: Figuring out how to connect with my fellow online swashbucklers was kind of a headache compared to the super-simplicity of Steam. It worked fine, it just wasn't smooth and easy, so anything that helps with that, I'm happy to take.

I'm less excited about the faster loading times. Not that I'm going to complain about performance improvements, I'm just not sure it matters in the grand scheme of things. When the Epic Games Store promised that its "vibe coded" launcher was faster than Steam, a common reaction was mockery: Much of that was sparked by Epic's insistent banging of the 'AI is inevitable' drum, but there was also a lot of 'who cares?' in the reactions, too. I think the Xbox PC app may face the same: Faster is good, sure, but is it going to convince many PC gamers to use it instead of Steam when they don't have to? Of this, I have doubts.
(Steam also recently dropped a performance update that promises to improve loading times as well, blunting the impact of both the Epic and Xbox boosts even further.)

If you want to check out the updated app for yourself, you'll need to be in the Xbox Insiders program—for that, you'll need to install the Xbox Insider Hub. A "refreshed Xbox web experience" is also on the way, with an improved library tab, more efficient use of screen space, and light, dark, and high-contrast visual modes.

articles.headline: Blue Origin's New Glenn launch delay will continue into 2027
keyFacts: Blue Origin's next New Glenn rocket launch is delayed until January 2027 following a launchpad explosion in May 2026.
CEO Dave Limp stated in an internal memo that weather issues caused infrastructure repairs to take longer than initially expected.
The Jeff Bezos-owned company holds upcoming contracts with NASA and Amazon that depend on the future rocket launches.
body: Blue Origin's New Glenn launch delay will continue into 2027
Repairs have been slow after an explosion earlier this year.

Blue Origin made waves earlier this year after a New Glenn rocket exploded on its launchpad in May 2026. This issue during a hot-test caused notable damage to the company's infrastructure in Florida that has delayed it from further activity. Shortly after the incident, Blue Origin's CEO claimed that the repairs would be finished quickly and that the next launch would occur before the end of the year. According to an internal memo from CEO Dave Limp, however, that timeline has been pushed back. The next rocket launch is now not expected until January 2027. Financial Times first reported on this development.

The memo suggests that the launchpad's Vehicle Access Tower has been repaired and restacked, and the launch bridge has been restored. Limp credited weather issues for the fixes happening slower than hoped. "Your collective work on our return to flight has been nothing short of remarkable," he wrote. "In just six months, Team Blue has accomplished what many thought would take years."

The company, owned by Jeff Bezos, is on the verge of notably expanding its footprint in space once it is cleared for takeoff again. Blue Origin won a contract from NASA in September to set up a telecommunications network for Mars. Its New Glenn rockets are also slated to bring more gear into space to support Amazon's Leo satellite broadband service.

articles.headline: The White House is apparently a popular residential proxy exit spot
keyFacts: Security firm Layer3 Intel reported that devices on the White House network were used as residential proxy exit nodes between October and November.
Layer3 founder Sergiy Usatyuk stated that infected devices, likely running a proxy SDK, created serious internal network security risks.
The US State Department requested Layer3 logs on Thursday, and Usatyuk reported that the proxy activity stopped Wednesday night.
body: Whether through malware or other means, devices associated with the White House network appear to be serving as residential proxy exit nodes, potentially posing security risks to one of the world's most sensitive networks.

News of the security snafu comes from security firm Layer3 Intel, which reported this week that it discovered the likely illicit activity thanks to its recently launched Residential Proxy Observatory . According to Layer3 founder Sergiy Usatyuk, the White House residential proxy activity might have gone unnoticed if not for the new tool.
“The observatory is just a public interface to explore the data we've been collecting for the past year,” Usatyuk told The Register in an email.

For those unfamiliar with residential proxies, they're like any old proxy network that obfuscates the location of a user, except in this case their exit nodes use IP addresses associated with residential internet connections, as opposed to datacenters. While many are legitimate, others are exploited by threat actors and used in the commission of cybercrimes, as the FBI warned earlier this year.

The FBI bulletin, put out in March, warns users to protect their systems against hijacking via malware, illicit SDK partnerships, VPNs with hidden service terms that repurpose user computers as exit nodes, and other threats used to turn victims into nodes without their consent.

Residential proxies are commonly used by threat actors to conceal command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, conduct phishing attacks, send spam, disguise malicious traffic, and the like, the FBI explained.

According to Layer3, its data shows 28 distinct residential proxy services exiting into the White House network nearly every day between October 5 and November 3, with 236 separate exits in that period. Other residential proxy detection services logged the same information, Layer3 said.

Most of the activity was happening in the evening, White House time, between 5 pm and midnight. That, Layer3 said, suggests someone at the White House - not a guest - has an infected device that’s serving as an exit, likely via an infected proxy SDK. If correct, that’s a problem.

“Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement,” Layer3 explained. “If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.”
In other words, this is a serious security risk, and one Usatyuk tells us could have been a problem for a while.

“Our data retention period goes back to July 10,” the Layer3 founder explained. “Given that there was continuous activity for a matter of months and other res proxy detection services independently verified the data, it's likely that White House IPs have been used by res proxy networks for all sorts of activity for some time now.”

Usatyuk said his firm’s data isn’t detailed enough to know how many machines are being used as exit nodes inside the White House network. He pointed us to an X post from security firm Synthient, which said it believes there are multiple Windows 10 and 11 devices on the White House network that likely have the Infatica SDK installed on them.

Infatica offers a software development kit (SDK) that allows app developers to monetize users' internet connections by turning their devices into residential proxy exit nodes. The possibility that this software is running on devices associated with the White House network raises serious security concerns: Vulnerable proxy software could potentially provide attackers with a route into internal systems.

Usatyuk told us that the most recent residential proxy activity on the White House network occurred Wednesday night, “hours after the blog went live,” but has since stopped. The US State Department contacted Layer3 Thursday morning to request a copy of the company’s logs, which Usatyuk tells us he’s sent over.
“Hopefully they've figured out the situation,” Usatyuk added - and hopefully before any government secrets have been exposed.
The White House didn't respond to questions for this story.®

articles.headline: Shares in Musk's SpaceX plunge as tech and AI stocks fall
keyFacts: SpaceX and Tesla shares dropped significantly as tech and AI stocks plummeted following the Democratic victory in the US midterm elections.
Investors are concerned about potential tougher scrutiny of data center construction and fears that AI infrastructure investments may not deliver expected returns.
Tech leaders including OpenAI's Greg Brockman acknowledged the need to improve communication regarding the benefits of AI and data centers to local communities.
body: - Published
Shares in Elon Musk's SpaceX have plunged as tech and artificial intelligence stocks more broadly plummeted a day after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterms.
Those losses dragged the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite stock index down, which had fallen by more than 5% at one point in early trading.
The market has been reacting to possible tougher scrutiny of data centre construction and the artificial intelligence (AI) industry following Democrat wins in key data centre states including Texas.
Following the election, some tech leaders have acknowledged they need to improve their communication around data centres and the benefits of AI.
SpaceX shares were down more than 9% in by lunchtime in Thursday trading, while Tesla shares dropped more than 11%.

Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas was turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday night.
Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned heavily against data centres, pledging a moratorium on new construction in the sector.
Shares in chipmakers have been suffering, with AMD dropping more than 14% on Thursday, while Micron shares had dropped by as much as 17% before recovering slightly.
Intel shares are down by more than 7% and shares in Nvidia have fallen nearly 9%, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had fallen by 10%.
The stock falls also hit the S&P 500 index, which dropped by 3.8% by lunchtime.
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said the steep sell-off on the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 was sending shockwaves into other markets.
"Fresh panic over the AI trade has hit Wall Street hard," she said.

"Fears that the vast sums poured into AI infrastructure may not deliver the returns investors have been banking on are now colliding with the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction."
Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms.
OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board.

"A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California on Wednesday evening.
Meta's president Dina Powell McCormick agreed that the industry needed to improve their communication about the benefits of AI.
"I think we need to double and triple down on telling the story," she told the WSJ conference.
Alongside the immediate impacts of the US mid-term elections, some investors have become concerned that AI shares could be in a bubble that is due a correction.
